items.question: How does the twofold unfolding power become the letter va?
premises: The unfolding power is twofold, like the will-power described before.
When it moves toward the power of otherness, it assumes a new form.
That form is the letter va, which pours forth the essence of creation.
items.inference: Therefore the twofold unfolding power, turning toward otherness, manifests as the letter va.
uncertainties: The exact nuance of sṛṣṭisāra as 'essence of creation' versus 'core flow of creation' is interpretive.
items.plain_english: In the same way, the twofold unfolding power, when it moves toward the power of otherness, becomes the letter va, which pours forth the essence of creation.

items.question: How do will, swiftness, shining, and firmness become air, fire, and earth?
premises: Will itself reaches the state of supreme bliss.
Through its association with swiftness it is called air.
Through shining and firmness it appears as fire and earth.
items.inference: Thus the same will-power differentiates into air, fire, and earth according to its modes.
uncertainties: The compound vahnirbhāsanātsthairyato is compressed; the distribution of bhāsanāt to fire and sthairyataḥ to earth follows the traditional reading.
items.plain_english: Will itself, having reached supreme bliss, is called air when joined with swiftness; through shining it becomes fire, and through firmness it becomes earth.

items.question: Why is this group of four said to be inner?
premises: This group of four is declared to be inner.
It is contained within will and the other powers.
It abides in its own completion.
items.inference: Therefore the group of four is called inner because it remains within will and rests in its own completion.
uncertainties: The exact referent of the 'group of four' is supplied by context rather than stated explicitly in this verse.
items.plain_english: This group of four is said to be inner because it is contained within will and the other powers and abides in its own completion.

items.question: What kind of joining is described for the powers of will and the rest?
premises: The powers beginning with will can be joined together.
This joining is described as consisting of agitation.
It applies both to same-kind powers and to those marked by agitation and nonagitation.
items.inference: Thus the joining of these powers is fundamentally an agitation.
uncertainties: The scope of kṣobhākṣobhātmanām is slightly ambiguous; it may refer to powers or to states.
items.plain_english: The joining of the same-kind powers, beginning with will, is said to be a form of agitation, and this also applies to those whose nature involves both agitation and nonagitation.

items.question: What two movements arise when the supreme meets its own sameness?
premises: When the supreme relates to its own sameness, a twofold movement arises.
One of these is simply the supreme itself.
That one can serve for the production of bliss.
items.inference: Therefore the supreme's self-relation yields two movements, one of which generates bliss.
uncertainties: The verse breaks mid-thought and continues into 161; the inference is limited to what is explicit here.
items.plain_english: When the supreme meets its own sameness, a twofold movement arises. One of these remains simply the supreme and can give rise to bliss.

items.question: What happens when the supreme joins in that bliss-producing movement?
premises: In that joining, a clearly agitated union arises.
Here too the supreme abode is present.
The second aspect is also for the purpose of production.
items.inference: Thus even the second movement of the supreme involves a clear agitation directed toward manifestation.
uncertainties: The sentence continues into 162; 'for producing' lacks an explicit object in this verse alone.
items.plain_english: In that joining, a clearly agitated union arises. Even here the supreme abode is present, and the second aspect also serves the purpose of bringing something forth.

items.question: When is the supreme nature insufficient without agitation?
premises: Without agitation, the supreme nature is not sufficient for manifestation.
Will may be devoid of action.
Will may also be tinged by what is to be willed.
items.inference: Therefore manifestation requires agitation, especially as will relates to action and its object.
uncertainties: aiṣṭavyena is rare in form; it is taken as the object to be willed.
items.plain_english: Without agitation, the supreme nature is not sufficient. Will may lack action, or it may be tinged by what is to be willed.

items.question: How does will become threefold through swiftness and firmness?
premises: Will is divided by swiftness and firmness.
Through this division it attains a threefold state.
These states are described as unopened, opening, and fully opened.
items.inference: Thus will differentiates into three stages of manifestation.
uncertainties: The subject 'will' is carried over from the previous verse rather than repeated.
items.plain_english: Divided by swiftness and firmness, will becomes threefold, appearing as unopened, opening, and fully opened.

items.question: Why does the willed object appear threefold within will?
premises: What is willed appears threefold within will.
Its essential form is not lost in that differentiation.
It is brought forth by will's own heat, which is the impulse of its freedom.
items.inference: Therefore the threefold willed object arises from will's own free, heated impulse without losing its identity.
uncertainties: svoṣmaṇā is metaphorical; 'heat' is kept literal but may imply inner potency.
items.plain_english: What is willed appears threefold within will without losing its essential form, brought forth by will's own inner heat, which is the impulse of its freedom.

items.question: How do the sibilants give rise to the manifest universe in the letter sa?
premises: The triad of śa, ṣa, and sa is projected outward clearly.
This projection stands as a manifest form.
From that, in the letter sa, the universe shines forth clearly.
items.inference: Therefore the outward projection of the sibilant triad culminates in sa, where the universe becomes manifest.
uncertainties: The sandhi in sakāre@sminsphuṭaṃ is irregular in the source; the intended reading is taken as 'in this letter sa clearly'.
items.plain_english: When the triad of śa, ṣa, and sa is clearly projected outward, it stands forth; and from that, in the letter sa, the whole universe shines clearly.

rows.gloss: in cessations of beginning-and-end of agitation

items.question: What do yogins recognize in the cessation of agitation?
premises: Yogins call that state the immortal supreme abode.
It is found in the cessations of the beginning and end of agitation.
That same state is also called the supreme nectar.
items.inference: Therefore the still point beyond agitation is identified as both supreme abode and supreme nectar.
uncertainties: The plural locative virāmeṣu may indicate repeated moments of cessation rather than distinct places.
items.plain_english: Yogins declare that this is the immortal, supreme abode. In the cessations at the beginning and end of agitation, that very state is known as the supreme nectar.

rows.gloss: in absorptions of hissing-sound bliss and true-being

items.question: How is that same nectar-state experienced in yogic absorption?
premises: That same state appears in absorptions marked by the hissing sound, bliss, and true being.
It is recognized in deep contemplative immersion.
Teachers declare it to be the supreme undivided absolute.
items.inference: Therefore the nectar-state is directly experienced as the supreme undivided absolute in certain absorptions.
uncertainties: sītkāra may refer to a subtle breath-sound; the gloss keeps it close to the literal term.
items.plain_english: In absorptions marked by the hissing sound, bliss, and the sense of true being, that very state is declared to be the supreme, undivided absolute.

items.question: Where did the Blessed Lord teach this doctrine of unity?
premises: The Blessed Lord himself spoke this teaching.
He spoke it in the glorious Kula mystery.
That text bears a true name gained from the unity of power and the holder of power.
items.inference: Thus the doctrine is grounded in an authoritative Kula scripture centered on the unity of Śakti and Śaktimat.
uncertainties: The exact title implied by kulaguhkare is not fully explicit; it is rendered descriptively.
items.plain_english: The Blessed Lord himself taught this in the glorious Kula mystery, a text whose true name arises from the unity of power and the holder of power.

items.question: What is the poison-principle revealed in that Kula teaching?
premises: The Lord revealed the poison-principle called anacka.
It is described as shaped like a crow's beak-cavity.
It is free from meditation and concentration and was revealed out of affection.
items.inference: Therefore the anacka poison-principle is a direct, non-methodic revelation within the Kula teaching.
uncertainties: The visual image of kākacañcupuṭa is symbolic; its precise experiential referent is not specified.
items.plain_english: Out of affection, he revealed to you the poison-principle called anacka, shaped like a crow's beak-cavity and beyond meditation and concentration.

items.question: How do desire and poison reveal their true principles?
premises: The fullness of desire is revealed in union.
The nectar-principle of poison is revealed when concealment falls away.
Both are disclosed through a change in how they are experienced.
items.inference: Therefore desire and poison disclose their highest principles when their limiting conditions are transcended.
uncertainties: The compound chādyatve@ṇoścyute is textually compressed; the reading 'when concealment of the limited one falls away' is interpretive.
items.plain_english: The true principle of desire is revealed as fullness in union, and the true principle of poison is revealed as nectar when concealment falls away.

items.question: Why is the pervading power called poison in relation to the supreme abode?
premises: The pervading power is called poison.
It covers the light of what does not pervade.
The supreme abode is stainless in itself, yet appears stained through that covering.
items.inference: Therefore the pervading power is termed poison because it veils the stainless supreme light.
uncertainties: avyāptuḥ is syntactically compressed; the contrast is read as between pervading power and the non-pervading or veiled state.
items.plain_english: The pervading power is called poison because it covers the light of what does not pervade. The supreme abode is stainless in itself, but in relation to that power it appears stained.

items.question: How are will, knowledge, and action identified with desire, poison, and the goddess?
premises: The universe is of the nature of action-power and flashes forth from that source.
Will is identified with desire.
Knowledge is identified with poison, and action is identified with the goddess, the stainless one.
items.inference: Therefore the triad of will, knowledge, and action appears as desire, poison, and the stainless goddess in manifestation.
uncertainties: The mapping of jñāna to viṣa is doctrinally specific; the verse states it but does not explain it.
items.plain_english: Because the universe, whose nature is action-power, flashes forth from that source, will is called desire, knowledge is called poison, and action is called the goddess, the stainless one.

items.question: What is the spiritual identity realized through absorption in this triad?
premises: Absorption in this triad is called Śiva, Bhairava.
The teachers instructed that one should become firmly established in it.
This establishment is to be maintained always.
items.inference: Therefore stable absorption in the triad of desire, poison, and the goddess is the realization of Bhairava.
uncertainties: The imperative sense of kuryāt is generalized; the verse gives instruction without specifying the subject.
items.plain_english: Absorption in this triad is called Śiva, Bhairava. Our teachers said that one should always become firmly established in that state.

items.question: What realization arises upon entering the poison-principle?
premises: One enters the poison-principle.
In that state there is no being, no poison, and no seizing force.
One should shine forth with the contemplation 'I alone'.
items.inference: Therefore entering the poison-principle culminates in the pure awareness of sole I-consciousness.
uncertainties: grahaḥ can mean a seizer or a possessing entity; the broader sense is retained.
items.plain_english: Having entered the poison-principle, one should shine forth with the contemplation 'I alone,' where there is no being, no poison, and no seizing force.

items.question: If origin is said to come from the ṣaṇṭha letters, how can ṣaṇṭha-ness apply here?
premises: An objection arises because origin is said to come from the ṣaṇṭha letters.
This seems to imply ṣaṇṭha-ness in the present case.
The reply is that the ṣaṇṭha is not the producer here.
items.inference: Therefore the presence of ṣaṇṭha letters does not make the ṣaṇṭha the generative principle in this context.
uncertainties: The technical term ṣaṇṭha is retained in transliteration because its doctrinal meaning is specific.
items.plain_english: An objection is raised: if origin is said to come from the ṣaṇṭha letters, how can ṣaṇṭha-ness apply here? The answer is that in this case the ṣaṇṭha is not the producer.

items.question: What actually produces the intended effect in that context?
premises: The will-power present there is the one that has been declared.
That same will-power produces its own task.
It does so inwardly, in the form of its own desired object.
items.inference: Therefore will-power, not the ṣaṇṭha, is the true producer of the effect.
uncertainties: tatragā is compact; it is read as qualifying the will-power operating in that locus.
items.plain_english: For the will-power present there is the one that has been declared, and that very will-power produces its own task inwardly, in the form of what it desires.

items.question: Why does the tinged aspect not count as the true source of production?
premises: What stands there as the cause of tinging is the object to be willed.
From that part there is no true production.
What arises from it is turbidity and its corresponding form.
items.inference: Therefore the tinged, object-side aspect yields turbidity, not the primary creative production.
uncertainties: eṣitavyam is read as the object to be willed; the syntax is compressed.
items.plain_english: What stands there as the cause of tinging is the object to be willed. From that aspect there is no true production; what arises from it is turbidity and its form.

items.question: Why is the ṣaṇṭha understood as a collective rather than a primary power?
premises: The ṣaṇṭha is joined with tinging from the knowable.
It has the nature of a collective.
It lacks the status of an abode that is either agitating or nonagitating in the primary sense.
items.inference: Therefore the ṣaṇṭha is a derivative collective, not a primary locus of agitation or stillness.
uncertainties: The long compound at the end is doctrinally dense; the gloss follows the most direct grammatical reading.
items.plain_english: They know the ṣaṇṭha as a collective joined with tinging from the knowable, because it does not function as a primary abode of either agitation or nonagitation.

items.question: Why was this group of four letters named ūṣma by Bhairava?
premises: This group of four letters shines through its own heat.
That shining is the basis of its designation.
Bhairava of pure nature declared its name to be ūṣma.
items.inference: Therefore the four letters are called ūṣma because their manifesting power is expressed as inner heat.
uncertainties: The referent 'group of four letters' is carried from the phonemic context rather than named explicitly in this verse.
items.plain_english: Because this group of four letters shines forth through its own inner heat, Bhairava of pure nature declared its name to be ūṣma.
